question: Which statement gives the full physics definition of work done on an object?
choices: Work is done whenever a force acts on an object, regardless of whether the object moves.
Work is any effort exerted by a person or machine, whether or not an object changes position.
Work is done on an object when a force acts on it while it undergoes a displacement, and depends on the component of the force along that displacement.
Work is the total distance an object travels while any force acts on it.

feedback.correct: Correct — Work requires both a force and a displacement, and only the force component along the displacement direction contributes — this is the complete definition.

incorrect.0: This is the misconception being tested directly — a force with no resulting displacement does zero work, regardless of how much effort it required.
incorrect.1: "Effort" is not a physics quantity; a force producing no displacement (e.g., pushing on an immovable wall) does no work no matter how much effort is exerted.
incorrect.3: Distance alone, without reference to force or its direction, cannot determine work; a force perpendicular to the entire path would do zero work despite nonzero distance traveled.

hint: Work $= F d$ only for the component of the force *along* the displacement. Force $\perp$ displacement ($90^\circ$) does zero work; force opposite the motion ($180^\circ$) does negative work.
solution: Work requires both a force and a displacement, and only the force component along the displacement direction contributes — this is the complete definition.
